title: Saul Meets the Risen Jesus
summary: Saul, carrying the high priest's letters to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus, is struck down by a light from heaven and hears Jesus ask why Saul persecutes him. Blinded, he is led into the city, where the Lord sends a reluctant disciple named Ananias to restore his sight; Saul is filled with the Spirit, baptized, and at once proclaims Jesus as the Son of God. After escaping plots in Damascus and Jerusalem he is sent to Tarsus, and the church enjoys peace while Peter heals Aeneas at Lydda and raises Tabitha at Joppa.
story: Saul first appeared holding the coats of those who stoned Stephen (7:58) and then leading the persecution that scattered the church (8:1-3). Now the persecutor is confronted by the one he persecutes. This is one of the most important turning points in the New Testament: the man who will carry the gospel to the Gentiles and write much of the New Testament is turned around on a road. Luke considers it so important that he tells it three times (here, in 22:3-16, and in 26:9-18). The chapter then returns to Peter, whose travels along the coast bring him to Joppa, where chapter 10 will begin with a vision that opens the door to the Gentiles.
historical:
Saul was a Jew from Tarsus, a leading city of Cilicia in southeastern Asia Minor, a Pharisee trained in Jerusalem under Gamaliel (22:3), and a Roman citizen by birth (22:28). His own letters describe his earlier zeal as a persecutor of the church (Galatians 1:13-14; Philippians 3:5-6). His conversion is usually dated to about AD 33 to 36. Damascus, an ancient city in Syria, lay roughly 135 miles or more northeast of Jerusalem, several days' travel. It had a large Jewish population and several synagogues. Straight Street, the main east-west street of the Roman city, is still traced in the old city today.

Paul's own account in Galatians 1:15-18 adds that after his conversion he went away into Arabia (probably the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Damascus) and returned to Damascus, and only after three years went up to Jerusalem. Luke compresses this period into many days (9:23). In 2 Corinthians 11:32-33 Paul says the governor under King Aretas (the Nabataean king Aretas IV) guarded the city to seize him, while Acts says the Jews plotted to kill him; the two accounts may describe different parties to the same danger. How much legal authority the high priest had over synagogues in Damascus is uncertain, but letters of recommendation and requests of this kind were common.
cultural:
The Way was one of the earliest names for the followers of Jesus (also 19:9, 23; 24:14), probably reflecting Jesus' teaching about the way of God, or his claim to be the way (John 14:6). It suggests a whole manner of life rather than a set of opinions. Being led by the hand into the city was a humiliation for a man who had set out with authority. Fasting for three days was a sign of deep distress or repentance.

Lydda (the old town of Lod) and Joppa (modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv) were towns on or near the coastal plain of Sharon, with a strong Jewish population. Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas is Greek; both mean gazelle, suggesting a community that used both languages. The widows showing Peter the clothes she had made shows her way of caring for the poor. Washing and laying out the body in an upper room was Jewish burial preparation. Peter's stay with a tanner is significant: tanners handled the skins of dead animals, which made them ritually unclean in the eyes of many, and their work was often looked down on. Peter's lodging there hints that his scruples are already loosening before his vision in chapter 10.
literary: The chapter has two parts, one about Saul (1-31) and one about Peter (32-43). The Saul story uses paired visions: Saul sees Ananias coming (9:12), and Ananias is told of Saul (9:10-16). Ananias's objection lets Luke underline the scale of the change. The persecutor who came to bind those who called on Jesus' name becomes one who calls on that name and will suffer for it. Luke places a summary at 9:31, the church in Judea, Galilee, and Samaria at peace and growing, which marks the completion of the second stage of 1:8. Peter's two miracles echo those of Jesus, especially the raising of Jairus's daughter, where Jesus took the girl by the hand and told her to get up (Mark 5:40-42); if Peter spoke in Aramaic, his command would have been Tabitha koum, one letter different from Jesus' words, Talitha koum.

outline.t: Saul on the road: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting
Saul's sight restored; filled with the Spirit and baptized
Saul preaches in Damascus and escapes in a basket
Barnabas vouches for Saul in Jerusalem; sent to Tarsus
Summary: the church at peace and growing

doctrines.note: Saul's conversion is entirely God's initiative. He is not seeking Jesus but hunting his followers when the risen Lord stops him. Paul would later describe himself as the foremost of sinners shown mercy as an example (1 Timothy 1:15-16). No one is beyond the reach of grace.

Jesus asks, why do you persecute Me? He so identifies with his people that to attack them is to attack him. This union of Christ and his church becomes a major theme of Paul's letters, where the church is Christ's body.

Saul is called to carry Jesus' name before the Gentiles and their kings and before the people of Israel. His calling includes suffering from the start. The mission to the nations now has its chief human instrument.

Ananias is sent so that Saul may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit, and Saul is baptized. Luke does not narrate the exact moment of the filling. The church's peace and growth are credited to the encouragement of the Holy Spirit (9:31).

words.note: Dioko, to pursue or persecute. The same verb can mean to chase after something good (Philippians 3:12, 14) or to hunt down someone for harm. Jesus uses it twice in 9:4-5: Saul is persecuting him. Later Paul himself will be persecuted in city after city, and he will describe his former life by this word (1 Corinthians 15:9; Galatians 1:13).

Skeuos, vessel, instrument, or tool. The Lord calls Saul a chosen instrument (literally a vessel of choosing). A vessel is made to carry something, and Saul will carry the name of Jesus. Paul later uses the same word when he says we have this treasure in jars of clay (2 Corinthians 4:7): the instrument is ordinary, the treasure is not.

Hodos, road or way. The word does double duty in this chapter: Saul seeks those who belong to the Way (9:2), and he meets Jesus on the road (9:17, 27). The early Christian movement was a way of living, and Saul discovers it on the road he was using to destroy it.

christ: The central event of the chapter is an appearance of the risen Jesus. Paul would later list this appearance with those to Peter, the Twelve, and James as a witness of the resurrection, calling himself one abnormally born (1 Corinthians 15:8). The light from heaven and the voice show Jesus as the exalted Lord, sharing God's glory. His words, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting, show his union with his people. Saul's first preaching sums up what he learned on the road: Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ. Through Peter, Jesus continues to heal and raise the dead (Jesus Christ heals you, Peter tells Aeneas), and many turn to the Lord. The chapter shows the living Christ turning his enemy into his servant and extending his life-giving power through his church.

hard.q: Was Saul converted from one religion to another, or called to a new task within the faith of Israel? And do the three accounts of it agree?
hard.a:
Some scholars, notably Krister Stendahl in Paul Among Jews and Gentiles (1976), have argued that Paul's experience should be understood as a prophetic call rather than a conversion, since Paul did not change gods or stop being a Jew, and he describes it in Galatians 1:15-16 in language that echoes the calls of Isaiah and Jeremiah. Others reply that it was both: Paul remained a Jew who worshiped Israel's God, but he turned from persecuting Jesus to worshiping him, and he later counted his former confidence as loss (Philippians 3:7-8). Most readers find both elements in the text.

The three accounts in Acts differ in detail. Here the companions hear the voice but see no one (9:7); in 22:9 they see the light but do not hear the voice of the one speaking. Many interpreters explain this as hearing a sound without understanding the words, a distinction the Greek can bear. In chapter 26 Paul's commission is spoken by Jesus himself on the road, while here it comes through Ananias. Ancient historians often varied the telling of an event to suit each audience, and Luke, who clearly knew all three versions, did not see them as contradicting one another. All agree on the core: a light, a voice, Jesus identified as the one Saul persecuted, and a commission to the Gentiles.

questions: Jesus said to Saul, why do you persecute Me? What does it mean to you that Christ takes the treatment of his people personally?
Ananias went to the man who had come to arrest him and called him Brother Saul. Whom might God be asking you to welcome whom you would rather avoid?
Barnabas vouched for Saul when others were afraid. Who has spoken up for you, and for whom could you do the same?
